papers.title: When is the deepest drawdown also the longest?
papers.abstract: Does the deepest drawdown take the longest to recover? For random walks with iid increments of positive finite mean, we find that the deepest and longest episodes are eventually distinct almost surely under light-tailed losses, but coincide with probability tending to one under heavy-tailed losses. More precisely, when losses have a finite exponential moment, the deepest episode's duration, relative to the longest among $n$ episodes, converges in probability to an explicit $\rho\in(0,1)$, while its descending duration rank is $n^{1-\rho+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)}$. These limits hold for every fixed number of leading depths; in the Gaussian model, $\rho=1/2$, independently of drift and variance. The separation reflects the different exponential costs of reaching a large depth and sustaining a long episode. For regularly varying losses, a common large loss governs both depth and duration: the duration ratio tends to one almost surely, and for every fixed $k$, the $k$ deepest and $k$ longest episodes have the same indices in the same order with probability tending to one. For any $k_n\to\infty$ with $k_n=o(n)$, the proportion of common episodes among the $k_n$ deepest and $k_n$ longest converges in probability to zero in the light-tailed case and to one in the heavy-tailed case. These ranking laws also hold for completed drawdowns within a deterministic observation horizon.

papers.title: Expected shortfall estimation and capital coverage under overlapping scenarios
papers.abstract: Expected shortfall (ES) is routinely estimated from a short sample of profit-and-loss (P&L) scenarios built from overlapping multi-day returns, while the non-parametric estimators applied to such data are designed under independent sampling. We study how this mismatch affects estimation accuracy and capital coverage, and how it interacts with serial dependence and heavy tails in the underlying P&L. Working within the coherent risk estimation framework, we compare six order-statistic-based ES estimators on fit, bias, and capital-coverage metrics. Following the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), we use a one-year estimation window and ES at the $2.5\%$ confidence level as a benchmark setup. We combine simulations with market data on twelve risk factors and ninety-nine equity portfolios. We show that overlapping sampling does not merely add noise but shifts ES estimates systematically downward, thereby weakening capital coverage. Serial dependence acts in the same direction, and heavy tails amplify both effects. More conservative weighting mitigates the underestimation but does not remove it. On market data, the confidence level at which the estimated capital covers realized losses roughly doubles in median under overlapping sampling for every estimator, while the $\textrm{ES}_{2.5\%}$-to-$\textrm{VaR}_{1\%}$ ratio, which links the FRTB base market risk capital metric to its pre-FRTB predecessor, changes comparatively little. Overlapping sampling can thus substantially understate ES-based capital. Since many banks apply a small set of standard estimators in their FRTB regulatory or economic capital model in a historical simulation approach, this understatement is likely to be common for many institutions, and combining simulation-based assessment of estimation risk with coverage-based diagnostics offers a practical method to detect it in model validation and monitoring.

papers.title: Joint Exclusivity
papers.abstract: We introduce \emph{joint exclusivity} (JE), a relaxation of mutual exclusivity (ME) for non-negative random vectors that forbids only the simultaneous positivity of all $n$ components. Whereas ME requires the probabilities of positive outcomes to sum to at most one, a JE random vector with prescribed marginals $F_1,\ldots,F_n$ exists if and only if $$ \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{F}_i(0)\le n-1. $$ An inclusion--exclusion identity shows that JE laws are determined by their $(n-1)$-dimensional margins and decomposes aggregate stop-loss premiums into those of sub-portfolios. A single wrap-around construction attains the existence bound, minimises the number of claims in convex order and, in frequency--severity models with exchangeable severities, the aggregate loss, extending the safest-dependence property of ME beyond its admissible range. We develop canonical and distortion-based constructions, an $m$-exclusivity hierarchy between ME and JE, and admissibility criteria for general families of claim patterns, explicit for hierarchical caps. Finally, we identify the most dangerous exclusive structure in convex order for lines sharing a severity law, which yields sharp stop-loss and Tail Value-at-Risk bounds.
